Pregnancy

Walking and exercise when expecting twins: make an individual plan

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

It is understandable to feel cautious about exercise when you are expecting twins. Many people can stay gently active, but the plan should fit the pregnancy and be reviewed when symptoms or circumstances change. Routine bed rest is not a proven way to prevent twins being born early.

Start with your pregnancy, not a blanket rule

Being pregnant with twins does not automatically mean giving up walking or spending the pregnancy in bed. Gentle movement may support comfort, mood and fitness. The safest plan depends on your health, symptoms, previous activity and the way this pregnancy is progressing.

Twin pregnancies have a higher risk of preterm birth and some other complications, so advice for an uncomplicated singleton pregnancy should not be copied without discussion. At an antenatal visit, ask which activities, intensity and duration suit you now and what would require a review. The answer can change as pregnancy progresses.

Why routine bed rest is no longer the default

Bed rest was once commonly recommended in multiple pregnancy to try to prevent early birth. Current SMFM guidance recommends against routine hospital admission and activity restriction solely for that purpose. It also advises against routinely restricting activity for a shortened cervix or symptoms of preterm labour as a prevention strategy.

Prolonged inactivity can contribute to loss of fitness, blood clots and emotional or practical difficulties. This does not mean ignoring an individual restriction or continuing exercise through symptoms. If you have been told to rest, ask what that means, why it was advised and when it will be reassessed. Ordinary breaks for comfort are different from prescribed prolonged bed rest.

Choose a manageable starting point

If your maternity team agrees, a short walk or another low-impact activity can be a starting point. Someone who was already active may be able to continue an adapted routine, while someone starting now should build up gently. Pregnancy is not the time to suddenly begin an unfamiliar strenuous programme.

There is no compulsory schedule of adding five minutes every week until you reach thirty minutes. General pregnancy exercise targets are a discussion point, not a minimum you must achieve while carrying twins. Shorter sessions with rests may be more comfortable. Choose an effort at which you can still talk, and stop if you feel unwell.

Expect the plan to change as your body changes

A growing abdomen, altered balance and fatigue can make familiar activities harder, particularly later in pregnancy. Some people need to slow down earlier than expected. That is a reason to adapt the activity, not evidence that they have failed to stay fit.

There is no universal rule that every twin pregnancy must stop all exercise at twenty-eight weeks. Your team may recommend limits for a particular complication or symptom. New or marked breathlessness, palpitations or exhaustion should be assessed rather than attributed automatically to carrying two babies. Anaemia is one possible contributor, but not the only explanation.

Walking can be flexible and accessible

Walking allows you to choose the route, pace and length without specialist equipment. Start on a level, familiar route where you can turn back easily. Comfortable footwear, access to water and breaks can make it more manageable. You do not need to finish a planned distance when your body asks you to stop.

Back, pelvic or knee pain may mean the route or activity needs changing; a physiotherapist can help with persistent symptoms. Walking cannot promise to prevent swelling, and the absence of joint pain is not the only safety check. Bleeding, contractions, dizziness and other warning symptoms matter too.

Swimming may reduce the feeling of weight on joints

Water supports your body, which can make gentle swimming or a suitable pregnancy water class comfortable. You can reduce speed, distance or the length of the session as needed. Take care getting in and out and on slippery pool surfaces.

Swimming is not automatically suitable through every complication. Check with your maternity team if you have bleeding, suspected leaking waters, illness or an exercise restriction. It may ease discomfort for some people, but it is not a guaranteed treatment for swelling or varicose veins. Avoid overheating and stop if you feel dizzy, breathless or unwell.

Adapt yoga to pregnancy and to your symptoms

A suitable pregnancy yoga class can combine gentle movement, breathing and relaxation. Tell the instructor that you are carrying twins and about any advice from your maternity team. Choose supported positions and avoid hot yoga, forceful stretching and positions that cause pain or make you feel faint.

There is no single fourteen-week starting rule that makes every yoga class safe. The type of class, instructor experience and your individual pregnancy matter. Positions lying on the abdomen become uncomfortable, and prolonged flat-back positions need modification as pregnancy progresses. Ask for alternatives rather than forcing your body into a pose.

Pilates needs suitable instruction and realistic expectations

Pregnancy-adapted Pilates may help with strength, posture and body awareness. An instructor experienced in pregnancy can change exercises as your balance and comfort change. Tell them about pelvic girdle pain, abdominal symptoms or medical restrictions before starting.

Breathe normally and avoid straining, overheating or continuing through pain. Long periods flat on your back may need changing, and some demanding abdominal exercises will not suit you. Pilates cannot guarantee a shorter, easier birth. A class should support your present comfort and function rather than promise a particular delivery outcome.

Pelvic floor work includes letting the muscles relax

The pelvic floor supports the bladder, bowel and womb. Pregnancy places extra demands on these muscles, and appropriately taught exercises can help with bladder control. Practise the gentle lift and squeeze together with complete release, while breathing normally.

If you cannot find the muscles, have pelvic pain or feel that tightening makes symptoms worse, ask for pelvic-health physiotherapy advice. More squeezing is not always the answer. Exercises may reduce some pelvic-floor problems, but they cannot guarantee that leakage or prolapse will never occur. They are one part of care, not a substitute for assessing symptoms.

Bleeding, placenta and cervical concerns need specific advice

New spotting or bleeding is a reason to stop exercise and contact maternity care. A low-lying placenta, placenta previa, a subchorionic haematoma, a short cervix or a history of preterm birth each deserves a discussion based on the actual findings. These labels do not all imply the same restriction.

Current contractions, suspected ruptured membranes or signs of preterm labour need assessment now. Do not use a general article to decide that exercise is safe through them. Equally, do not assume strict bed rest has been proved to prevent miscarriage, stop cervical shortening or prevent early delivery. Ask for a precise plan for daily movement, exercise, work and follow-up.

Blood pressure, anaemia and other complications also change the assessment

High blood pressure or pre-eclampsia, troublesome low blood pressure with faintness, severe anaemia, and heart or lung disease may affect what activity is appropriate. The degree of illness and symptoms matter. These conditions need their own care; simply staying in bed is not their treatment.

Concerns about either baby’s growth also require specialist monitoring and individual advice. Evidence does not establish routine activity restriction as an effective treatment for fetal growth restriction or hypertensive disease. Your team may still advise stopping a particular exercise while investigating or managing a problem. Clarify what remains safe rather than guessing from a diagnosis alone.

Know which symptoms mean stopping and getting help

Stop and contact maternity triage promptly for bleeding, possible fluid leakage, regular or painful contractions, new pelvic pressure, concerning back or abdominal pain, dizziness, blurred vision, severe headache or sudden marked swelling of the face or hands. A change or reduction in your babies’ usual movements needs immediate maternity advice; do not wait until the next day.

Chest pain, collapse, severe breathlessness or severe persistent abdominal pain needs emergency assessment. A painful, swollen, red or warm calf (especially on one side) also needs urgent assessment for a possible clot. New palpitations with chest pain, faintness or breathing difficulty are urgent. These signs matter whether you are exercising or resting.

Mild ankle swelling can happen during pregnancy, but sudden, one-sided or painful swelling is different. If you feel unusually unwell or uncertain about a symptom, call your maternity service. Do not finish the workout first or rely on resting to prove that everything is fine.

Make the plan practical enough to follow

Keep water available, avoid overheating and allow time for regular meals and rest. Choose activities with a low risk of falling or a blow to the abdomen. Supportive clothing, a nearby place to sit and help with other physical demands may matter more than meeting a daily exercise total.

At follow-up, describe what you actually do, how you feel during it and any symptoms afterwards. Ask whom to call between visits and when to reconsider the plan. A useful activity plan gives you permission to adapt while keeping warning signs and your babies’ monitoring in view.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

SMFM guidance, reaffirmed in 2025, opposes routine activity restriction to prevent preterm birth in multiple pregnancy.

Activity choice and limits still require assessment of complications, symptoms and the individual pregnancy.

How BeMama can help

Ask for a clear activity plan covering exercise, everyday tasks, warning symptoms and when the plan will be reviewed.

When to seek help

Maternity and physiotherapy review remain pending. New warning symptoms require assessment, not an experiment with a different exercise.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Twins do not automatically require bed rest.
  • Gentle activity can be adapted to comfort and medical advice.
  • There is no universal twenty-eight-week stop date.
  • Stop and seek advice for warning symptoms, including changed movements.

Frequently asked questions

Does carrying twins mean I must stay in bed?

No. Routine bed rest is not recommended solely to prevent preterm birth in multiple pregnancy. Ask about the reason and scope of any individual restriction.

Can I walk if I was not active before pregnancy?

Often a short gentle walk is an option after discussing your pregnancy and health with the maternity team. Build up only as comfortable and advised.

Must I reach thirty minutes every day?

No. A general activity target is not a requirement for every twin pregnancy. Shorter sessions or a different plan may suit you.

Should all exercise stop after twenty-eight weeks?

There is no universal rule. Your symptoms, complications and maternity advice determine what remains appropriate.

Is swimming always safe with twins?

No activity is suitable through every complication. Ask for advice with bleeding, suspected leaking waters, illness or a restriction.

Does yoga become safe automatically at fourteen weeks?

No. Class type, pregnancy adaptations and your individual circumstances matter more than a single starting date.

Will Pilates guarantee an easier birth?

No. It may support strength and comfort, but it cannot promise a particular labour or delivery.

Should I keep tightening my pelvic floor if it hurts?

No. Stop and ask for pelvic-health advice. Correct relaxation and an individual assessment are important too.

Can I wait until tomorrow if the babies move less?

No. Contact maternity care immediately for a change or reduction in usual movements. Do not wait for an appointment or the next day.

What should I ask when told to rest?

Ask which movements and tasks are limited, why, for how long, what symptoms need help and when the restriction will be reviewed.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
